findings.title: State-changing entry point without caller authorization
findings.description: A public contract function mutates storage but does not call require_auth or require_auth_for_args anywhere in its body or in the intra-file helper functions it calls. Without an authorization check, any account can invoke the function and change contract state, which may allow theft, privilege escalation, or corruption of contract data. This is a heuristic: authorization may legitimately be enforced by a callee or be intentionally absent for permissionless operations.
findings.evidence: `set` storage mutation with no authorization in `set_admin`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& symbol_short ! ("ADMIN") , & new_admin)
findings.remediation: Call `address.require_auth()` (or `require_auth_for_args`) for the account that must approve the operation before mutating state. Prefer authorizing a specific argument that binds the approval to the operation rather than authorizing a stored admin address unconditionally. If the function is intentionally permissionless, document that and suppress this rule for the function.

Overlong literals do not describe the symbol the author expects once truncated or fail to compile, while caller-built short symbols can deliberately collide with another key and overwrite or misread storage. This is a syntactic heuristic and reports medium confidence.
findings.evidence: unsafe short symbol in entry point `store`: `symbol_short!("this_is_too_long")` is 16 characters, longer than the 9-character short-symbol limit
findings.remediation: Use a constant literal of at most nine characters such as `symbol_short!("transfer")`, or use `Symbol::new(&env, value)` for longer or dynamic values. Never derive a storage key directly from caller input; map it through an allowlist of known keys.

findings.title: Unbounded string/bytes persisted from caller input
findings.description: Persisting a caller-controlled `String` or `Bytes` value without a length check lets an attacker grow ledger entries without bound, raising rent and potentially exceeding limits. The detector looks for a visible `.len()` comparison guarding the write.
findings.evidence: user-controlled `String` parameter `name` persisted without a length bound in `set_name`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& DataKey :: Name , & name)
findings.remediation: Reject or truncate values above an explicit maximum before persisting them (for example `if value.len() > MAX { return Err(...) }`). Storing a fixed-size hash instead of the raw value is usually safer.

findings.title: Ignored cross-contract call result
findings.description: A cross-contract client call is used as a bare statement, so its `Result` is discarded instead of being propagated with `?`, matched, or checked with `if let`. A failed call then looks successful to the caller, which can leave accounting, balances, or emitted state inconsistent. The detector only reports calls whose result is discarded; calls assigned, returned, or handled are ignored.
findings.evidence: cross-contract client call result is discarded in `withdraw`: client . transfer (& env . current_contract_address () , & token , & amount)
findings.remediation: Handle the client call result: propagate it with `?`, match on `Ok`/`Err`, use `if let`, or explicitly document and log an intentional ignore. Never leave a fallible cross-contract call as a bare statement or in `let _ =`.

findings.description: A public contract entry point is named like a test or debug backdoor (a `test`, `debug`, `dev`, `mock`, or `dummy` name segment). findings.title: Authorization check inside a loop
findings.description: A contract entry point performs `require_auth` (or `require_auth_for_args`) inside a loop body in a position that does not clearly cover every iteration: the check is conditional, or it runs only after a state-changing operation. A single check in that position can leave later iterations or earlier side effects unauthorized. Unconditional checks at the top of a loop are ambiguous and are deliberately not reported by this rule.
findings.evidence: `admin . require_auth ()` inside `for` loop at line 12 in entry point `batch_conditional` is conditional, so iterations that skip the branch are not authorized; one check may not be sufficient: admin . require_auth ()
findings.remediation: Authorize the actor before any state change and outside any conditional branch that can skip iterations, or authorize each distinct actor explicitly for every loop item with `require_auth_for_args`. Document intentional per-item authorization.

findings.title: Authorization after state mutation
findings.description: A contract entry point mutates storage before calling `require_auth`. The authorization check must run before the effect, otherwise a rejected call may already have changed state on some paths and the ordering indicates a logic bug.
findings.evidence: storage mutation before authorization in `batch_after_write`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (recipient , & 1)
findings.remediation: Authorize the caller at the start of the entry point, before any storage read or write that depends on the caller. Call `require_auth` or `require_auth_for_args` first, then perform the state change.

findings.title: Persistent storage read without TTL management
findings.description: A contract entry point reads persistent storage but does not call `extend_ttl`, `set_ttl`, or `bump` in the same function or in the intra-file helpers it calls. Persistent entries expire; if the read assumes the value is still present, an expired entry can change the contract's behaviour or block an operation that depends on it. The detector reports only when no TTL management is visible at all: a TTL call for an unrelated key is treated as ambiguous and suppresses the finding.
findings.evidence: persistent storage read without TTL extension in `balance`: env . storage () . persistent () . get (& symbol_short ! ("BAL"))
findings.remediation: Refresh the entry's time-to-live when reading persistent data that must remain available, for example `env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(&key, threshold, extend_to)` after the read. Prefer one documented TTL policy per contract. If TTL is managed by a separate maintenance entry point, suppress this rule for the reader with a justification.

findings.title: Unchecked arithmetic in a contract entry point
findings.description: A public contract entry point performs binary arithmetic (`+`, `-`, or `*`) on values without a checked, saturating, overflowing, or wrapping operation. In release builds Rust arithmetic wraps on overflow and underflow instead of panicking, so a decrement below zero (or an overflow) can silently produce an incorrect result — a common cause of balance and accounting bugs in token, escrow and vault contracts. This is a heuristic: it cannot prove that the operands are attacker-influenced or that their range is constrained, so it reports low confidence and should be reviewed in context.
findings.evidence: unchecked `-` arithmetic in entry point `withdraw`: balance - amount (use `checked_sub` and handle `None`)
findings.remediation: Use explicit checked arithmetic (`checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_mul`) and handle the `None` case with a typed contract error, or use saturating/overflowing variants when that semantics is intended. Prefer checked operations for balances, amounts, and counters derived from user input.

findings.title: Token transfer amount without validation
findings.description: A public contract entry point passes a caller-supplied amount to `transfer` or `transfer_from` without comparing it against zero. Token implementations differ in how they treat negative or out-of-range amounts; a missing guard can therefore move an unintended value, corrupt accounting, or revert in surprising ways. This is a heuristic: it cannot prove that the token rejects the value or that another layer validates it, so it reports low confidence.
findings.evidence: `transfer` transfers unchecked amount `amount` in entry point `payout`
findings.remediation: Validate the amount before transferring, for example reject `amount <= 0` with a typed contract error (or check both bounds when the token has a maximum). Validate once at the entry point and pass the checked value to `transfer`/`transfer_from`.

findings.title: Cross-contract call with an unvalidated address argument
findings.description: A cross-contract token call receives an address argument that originates from a caller-supplied parameter and was not passed through a documented address-validation helper. The scanner cannot prove the address is the expected account or contract, so a caller may direct a transfer, approval, mint, or burn at an unintended destination. Flows with more than one origin, or validation that happens only on some paths, are recorded as ambiguous by the taint analysis and are not reported.
findings.evidence: cross-contract `transfer` passes caller-controlled address argument 2 from `to` without documented validation in `payout`
findings.remediation: Validate the address before the cross-contract call. Use a documented helper such as `validate_address`, compare against an address stored at configuration time, or reject addresses that are not on an explicit allowlist. Validate on every path, before the call.

findings.title: Security check unreachable on every path
findings.description: A caller-authorization or validation check appears after a statement that always leaves the function, such as an unconditional `return`. No execution path reaches the check, so it provides a false sense of protection while the actual behaviour is unguarded. The detector reports only when the function's control-flow graph is complete: a truncated graph or one containing constructs the builder does not model suppresses the finding.
findings.evidence: `require_auth` check at line 13 in `set` is unreachable: every path leaves the function first (nearest `return` at line 12); CFG is complete (6 nodes, 5 edges, no unknown nodes)
findings.remediation: Remove the dead check or move it before the early return so every path that performs the sensitive operation is guarded. If the early return is intentional, make the guard part of the condition that returns instead of leaving unreachable code behind.

findings.title: Persistent storage write without TTL management
findings.description: A contract entry point writes to persistent storage but does not call `extend_ttl`, `set_ttl`, or `bump` in the same function or in the intra-file helpers it calls. Persistent entries have a time-to-live; if it is not extended, stored data can expire and be lost. TTL may legitimately be managed elsewhere (for example in a separate maintenance entry point), so this is a low-confidence signal.
findings.evidence: persistent storage write without TTL extension in `set_admin`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& symbol_short ! ("ADMIN") , & new_admin)
findings.remediation: When writing persistent data that must survive, extend its time-to-live with `storage().persistent().extend_ttl(...)` after the write. Prefer a single, well-documented TTL policy for the contract. If TTL is managed centrally, suppress this rule for the function.

findings.title: Privileged state change without an event
findings.description: A contract entry point mutates a storage key that looks like privileged configuration (for example admin, owner, pause, params, fees, or oracle) without publishing an event. Off-chain indexers and users rely on events to observe critical changes; without one, the change is invisible to monitoring and incident response.
findings.evidence: privileged storage change without an event in `set_admin`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& symbol_short ! ("ADMIN") , & new_admin)
findings.remediation: Publish an event with `env.events().publish(...)` for every privileged state change, including the old and new values where practical. Keep the event schema stable so indexers can rely on it.
